asr.full_text: every time the price is down someone somewhere is going to try to rationalize it right like it's because of this specific reason and i don't necessarily think that's the case sometimes the market just can be irrational um people are overexposed for various reasons or they're trying to use bitcoin as a hedge because they're worried about macro economic factors like war which doesn't make sense because, you know, they don't understand Bitcoin is not tech stock, but they're dumping stuff ahead of time because bitcoin is a more liquid market and is 24 seven and global. We're going to get nation state FOMO and then retail FOMO and all of that suing to mean a very steep adoption curve. You're going to feel it and it's going to happen faster than most people believe. There's hundreds of millions of dollars being purchased on an almost daily basis. Why isn't the price exploding? This market analysis might be one of the most insightful and important updates Samson Mou has shared in a long time. That's exactly why I'm bringing it to you today, as he breaks down why Bitcoin remains stuck around the $77,000 level, instead of pushing higher. He explains the key factors currently at play and what could eventually trigger the next wave of FOMO, sending prices to extreme levels. As short-term participants begin leaving the market, conditions may start to shift significantly. So let's dive in and hear his perspective. So it's just used as a dumping ground. But I see that it's coming to a close because traditional markets are becoming 24-7, and they're even trying to tokenize and launch on various blockchains, too. So there won't be a real need to dump bitcoin ahead of bad news to hedge anymore. And you couple that with the massive amount of buying demand from Strategy, from STRC, and other companies, that's not really a bearish thing that the tourists leave and the people with a plan and long-term outlook are coming in. Bitcoin price is affected by macro. It's like we are integrated into the financial system now through all these different instruments, ETFs, like TRAD Phi, futures markets, everything like that. So there is no separating Bitcoin. We've definitely grown up and we've grown into a place in the financial system, which I think is only going to get bigger and bigger as people understand Bitcoin. But if you look at the war playing out is definitely very interesting on a number of fronts. So you've seen that Iran is, they've been rumored to be taking Bitcoin for payment along with stable coins and Chinese Yen. But I don't think we've seen any confirmation yet, like no address has been publicized, that this is a Bitcoin address that's going to Iran. But the interesting thing there, less so for Bitcoin, more so for stable coins, is that Iran is seemingly accepting payment in stablecoins. And this is a very unique time in the history of the Federal Reserve, which is saying they are. They're seeing a decrease in demand for treas's and the US dollar in general as the world becomes multi polar and nations are going off the dollar or being forced off the dollar like in the case of Russia but to make up for that shortfall they've kind of embrace stablecoins so they passed a genius act act they're pushing stablecoins heavily a number of countries are but they need that to offset that drop in demand. Stablecoins for the most part are somewhat permissionless. They can be frozen but for a certain amount of time they can move freely, and if Iran is accepting stablecoins for payments, then it's sort of like, Do I want the dollar to live or control the dollar? Because if you start to block that rail then definitely Iran will move to a neutral money like Bitcoin. And I think this is an interesting precipice to be standing on to watch what the world chooses to do. I really can't figure out either way which one they're going to go with, so I'm watching along with everyone else. But it's definitely very entertaining to watch this dilemma unfold in real time. I do worry that there are misaligned incentives that Bitcoin developers want to keep developing. And if that is the case, and if there is enough people of that same mindset, then if you look at the whole spam war thing, it is very easy for them to waive a change through and just call a consensus. And I think a lot of core supporters, maybe yourself included, they don't really think about it from this perspective because they know the people, they like them and they kind of give them a free pass. And they think, well, it's a complete meritocracy, but if you look at this discourse, it's like people were saying, we should do something because it's spam and we should have this filter and we should not increase the opertern. And first they block people out of the chat on GitHub saying it's not the place to have a technical discussion. But then, where is the discussion to be held? Because now that they're blocked from discussing on GitHub, it has moved to X and maybe other platforms. Then they just discard it and say, well, that's just social media chatter and it's just bots and stuff like that. Who knows? But it's very easy to construct consensus in a number of ways. And just say, Well, the technical reason is this, and we decided we're going to do this. I think even some people that are very staunch core supporters did say, Well, they didn't have to remove the operatron limit, because it didn't really do anything. If you know how to bypass it, you can bypass it. But changing the default does change things materially because if the mining pool upgrades, which they are going to do because they want the security fixes and optimizations, they take that new default and they may not change it back, right? So the defaults have a lot of weight in this matter and how the network evolves and progresses. So back to the original point, I do think it's you need an implementation that says we're conservative. We don't really want changes. We want to ossify and focus on the use of Bitcoin as money. Now, the challenge is what is Bitcoin is money, because for a developer, Bitcoin is money is something I could program and get money out of it too. So for a developer, Bitcoin is money is a way that I can program and do a lot of things with. For a less technical person, Bitcoin is money is just sending a Bitcoin transaction or buying Bitcoin and putting it into cold storage. Saylor had a good point about this, he was saying if I wanted to attack the Bitcoin protocol I would just give developers unlimited capital, and he's famously not given grants to Bitcoin development. Probably for that reason, because if you give developers unlimited capital and leeway and they have the ability to manufacture their own consensus in their own circle, that's kind of a dangerous thing for Bitcoin. For the same reasons, we don't support a rapid patch to fix Bitcoin for quantum computing relevant computers and attack factor on that front. We should also not quickly push for some fork to limit spam because there is no rush. The damage is done already and the fix is long term. The fix is not a short-term quick thing Samson Moe continued to clearly explain that bitcoin could be affected by broader economic rotation shifts especially since it's still treated as a risk asset that's exactly why staying informed and understanding market movements is so important so you can position yourself ahead by allocating more capital wisely and keeping some cash on the side to take advantage of dips when opportunities appear. You need to avoid rushing in or chasing hype. Don't FOMO. Stay calm, think deeper, and focus on the long-term. As Samson Mao emphasized, hold as long as you can, and as much as you can, because years down the line, you'll likely thank yourself for not selling too early during uncertain market conditions.
